    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that clinically reviewed by Dr.
    • In a recent development, the benefits of meditation can reach across your well-being, from reducing stress and anxiety to improving focus and supporting mental and emotional health.
    • Recent findings suggest that we’ve grouped the many types of meditation into six families, so you can see how they relate before you pick one.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, CDCES, MBA.

    In a recent development, the benefits of meditation can reach across your well-being, from reducing stress and anxiety to improving focus and supporting mental and emotional health. But there’s a catch: meditation is a wide family of practices, and the type that works beautifully for your friend might leave you fidgety and frustrated.

    Recent findings suggest that we’ve grouped the many types of meditation into six families, so you can see how they relate before you pick one. Think of it as a menu. Try whichever one draws you in, and let your practice change as you do.

    Meditation is a way to train our attention and awareness so we can be more present in the moment. Most types ask you to rest your focus somewhere, like the breath, a word, a sensation, or a movement, and to notice without judgment when your mind drifts, then return. That returning, over and over, is the practice.

    What changes from one type to the next is where you place your attention and what you hope to cultivate. Some practices sharpen focus, while others cultivate compassion or help the body relax. Many share a thread of mindfulness, noticing where your attention drifts and gently coming back.

    With a history rooted in the spiritual traditions of the East, including Buddhism, Hinduism, and Taoism, meditation has long been recognized as a means to gain enlightenment, self-realization, and balance.

    By exploring the different forms of meditation practice, you can discover what works best for you to enhance your overall well-being.

    Industry observers note that these practices share a common aim. You anchor your attention in the present moment and meet whatever arises without judgment. They're a good place to start if you're new to meditation.

    Industry observers note that particularly accessible to beginners, mindfulness meditation invites you to immerse yourself in the present moment. It teaches you to observe your thoughts, feelings, and physical sensations without judgment. By focusing on the breath or the sensations in the body, rather than worries about the past or future, you learn to anchor yourself in the now. This can lead to reduced stress and improved well-being.

    Read more: How to practice mindfulness meditation: 8 tips to get started.

    Sources indicate that A body scan moves your attention slowly through the body, one area at a time, noticing sensation without trying to change it. It's a core mindfulness technique and a gentle way into the practice, since you always have your body to come back to. Many people use it to unwind before sleep.

    Read more: Body scan meditation: a step-by-step guide to practice.

    Industry observers note that here the breath is your anchor. You rest your attention on each inhale and exhale, without trying to control the rhythm, and return to it whenever your mind wanders. Because your breath is always with you, this is one of the most portable practices you can carry into a stressful moment.

    Read more: How to practice breath meditation to relieve stress.

    Sources indicate that mindful eating brings full attention to a meal through the senses: the color, smell, texture, and taste of your food, and the signals of hunger and fullness. It can support digestion and help you notice emotional eating patterns with more kindness.

    Read more: How mindful eating can boost your mental and physical health.

    In a recent development, focus is the whole point here. You rest your attention on one thing, a flame, a sound, or a word, and return to it each time the mind strays. Over time this can sharpen your attention and prepare you for deeper states.

    Industry observers note that concentration meditation is a practice of focused attention, where the mind is directed toward a single point of reference, such as a candle flame, a sound, or the breath. This can help develop focus and attentiveness in everyday life and prepare the mind for deeper states of meditation. This practice can be especially helpful for students, professionals, or anyone looking to improve their cognitive abilities and productivity.

    Read more: Concentration meditation: what is it and how to practice?

    According to recent reports, mantra meditation involves the silent repetition of a word or phrase, known as a mantra, to focus the mind and bring deeper states of meditation. This practice can be found in many spiritual traditions worldwide and serves as a powerful tool for calming the mind, reducing stress, and enhancing spiritual growth and a sense of peace and clarity. If you find yourself easily distracted or struggling with a busy mind, mantra meditation can help you maintain focus.

    Read more: Mantra meditation: what it is, benefits, and how to practice.

    Om meditation is a form of mantra practice built around chanting or silently repeating the sound "Om." The vibration of the sound gives the mind something to settle on, and many practitioners find the repetition grounding.

    Read more: What is Om meditation? Plus, a step-by-step guide to practice.

    Also called trataka, candle meditation uses the soft glow of a flame as your focal point. You rest your gaze on the candle, placed at eye level a short distance away, and let it hold your attention. It's a visual anchor for anyone who finds eyes-closed practice restless.

    Read more: Candle meditation: a step-by-step guide to practice at home.

    According to recent reports, visualization meditation guides you to picture a scene, place, or outcome in vivid detail, such as somewhere you feel calm and safe. By giving the mind a rich image to rest on, it can lower stress and support a sense of ease. Unlike open mindfulness, it actively directs the imagination.

    Read more: Visualization meditation: 8 exercises to add to your practice.

    Warmth is the thread running through this family, directed toward yourself, the people you love, and even those you struggle with. These practices can enhance empathy and strengthen your relationships.

    Recent findings suggest that compassion meditation aims to cultivate feelings of love, kindness, and compassion toward yourself and others. It involves silently directing sentiments of goodwill toward loved ones, acquaintances, and even people we might have a difficult relationship with. It encourages us to see beyond our differences, nurturing a sense of connectedness. A traditional example is Tonglen, a Tibetan practice that pairs the breath with compassion for suffering.

    Read more: Compassion meditation: what it is, benefits, & how to practice.

    Recent findings suggest that 11. Loving-kindness meditation (metta).

    It has been revealed that loving-kindness, or Metta meditation, is a practice of cultivating an attitude of unconditional love and kindness towards all beings. It starts with developing a loving acceptance of yourself and gradually extends outward to include friends, family, strangers, and even those with whom we may have conflicts. This practice can help break down barriers of anger and division, promoting peace and connection. Though loving-kindness meditation and compassion meditation are closely related and often practiced together, loving-kindness meditation involves sending wishes of happiness, well-being, and peace to yourself and others, whereas compassion meditation specifically focuses on suffering, understanding it, feeling it, and wishing for it to be alleviated.

    Read more: Loving-kindness meditation: what it is, how to practice and why.

    Sources indicate that gratitude meditation guides your attention toward what you appreciate, often by calling to mind a few people or moments you're thankful for. Practiced in the morning or evening, it can lower anxiety and support better sleep, and it pairs naturally with compassion practice.

    Read more: How gratitude meditation can help reduce anxiety.

    Sitting still doesn't suit everyone. If stillness makes you restless, these practices let you meditate while the body is in motion, with your attention on each movement.

    Moving meditation brings together deliberate movement and a focused mind. You move with purpose, noticing each step, stretch, or breath as you go. Yoga, tai chi, mindful stretching, and mindful dancing all fall under this heading, and it can be done almost anywhere.

    Read more: The benefits of moving meditation and how to start practicing.

    Sources indicate that walking meditation means walking slowly and deliberately, with your attention fully on the act of walking: each step, the movement of your legs, the ground beneath your feet, and your breath. It turns an everyday activity into a practice you can take outdoors.

    Read more: Walking meditation: how to practice and its benefits.

    Recent findings suggest that mindful movement is the broad practice of bringing present-moment awareness to how your body moves, whether through stretching, yoga, or simple everyday motion. It's mindfulness carried into the body rather than held in stillness.

    Read more: What is mindful movement? Plus 9 ways to get started.

    According to recent reports, qigong is a traditional Chinese practice that combines movement, breathwork, and meditation to support balance and focus. In its active form you meditate while flowing through slow, deliberate movements, which makes it a bridge between exercise and stillness.

    Read more: What is qigong? Benefits, types, and how to practice.

    Yoga nidra, sometimes called yogic sleep, is a guided rest practice done lying down. A teacher or recording leads you through stages of body scan, breath, and visualization into a state between waking and sleep. No yoga experience is needed, and it's often used for deep rest at bedtime.

    Read more: What is yoga nidra? Plus, why it may be your fresh BFF at bedtime.

    A few practices are rooted in a specific lineage and tend to go deeper, often taught within a tradition or by a teacher. Several come from Buddhism, while others, like Transcendental Meditation and kundalini, come from Hindu and Vedic traditions.

    It has been revealed that buddhist meditation is the broad tradition behind many of the best-known techniques, including Zen and Vipassana below, along with loving-kindness. If you want a feel for the tradition as a whole before exploring the specific practices, start here.

    Read more: Buddhist meditation: types, techniques & how to practice.

    Recent findings suggest that zen meditation, or Zazen, is a disciplined form of meditation central to Zen Buddhism. You sit in a specific posture, focusing on the breath while observing thoughts and sensations as they arise and pass without attachment. Zazen emphasizes the importance of moment-to-moment awareness for a profound sense of peace and insight.

    Read more: Zen meditation: how (and why) to start a Zen practice.

    Vipassana, which means "to see things as they really are," is one of India's most ancient techniques of meditation. It focuses on the deep interconnection between mind and body. Through disciplined attention to physical sensations, you can develop insight into the nature of impermanence, suffering, and egolessness, to move toward enlightenment and liberation. Vipassana meditation is challenging, yet rewarding, offering profound insights into our own minds.

    Read more: Vipassana meditation: what it is, benefits & how to practice.

    Sources indicate that 21. Transcendental Meditation (TM).

    Transcendental Meditation comes from the Hindu and Vedic tradition and was brought to the West in the mid-20th century. It's a silent, mantra-based practice, typically done for about 20 minutes twice a day, and it's taught one-on-one by a certified teacher who gives you your mantra. It's described as effortless, letting the mantra gently carry the mind toward deep rest.

    Read more: Transcendental Meditation versus mindfulness meditation.

    Kundalini meditation is a spiritual practice that aims to awaken what the tradition describes as an inner energy at the base of the spine, using breathwork, posture, and chanting. Practitioners describe effects in spiritual and energetic terms, which are rooted in belief rather than established science. Because the breathwork can be intense, check with your doctor first if you have respiratory, heart, or blood pressure concerns.

    Read more: What is Kundalini meditation? Plus, how to try it yourself.

    Recent findings suggest that chakra meditation focuses attention on the body's energy centers, or chakras, often by visualizing each as a spinning wheel, chanting a sound for each one, or breathing into each area. As with kundalini, the idea of chakras comes from spiritual tradition and is described as belief rather than scientific fact.

    Read more: Chakra meditation: what it is, benefits & how to practice.

    This family works from the body inward. The practices help your nervous system slow down and your muscles release tension, which makes them a good entry point when stress reveals up physically.

    According to recent reports, relaxation meditation is an umbrella term for any practice that helps the body release tension and the mind wind down. It often draws on breathing, body awareness, or guided sessions, and it's a gentle place to begin if deeper practices feel like a lot right now.

    A sound bath, where you lie back and listen to instruments, is one example.

    Read more: 5 relaxation meditations that actually work.

    25. Progressive muscle relaxation.

    According to recent reports, progressive muscle relaxation guides you to tense and then release each muscle group in turn, usually working from the feet up to the face. By targeting the physical side of stress, it can ease tension that anxiety stores in the body, and it pairs well with a body scan to finish.

    Read more: What is progressive muscle relaxation (and how to practice it).

    The six families above group the 25 types by where your attention goes. This table puts them side by side, so you can compare meditation types and see where to start.

    Sources indicate that there’s no one-size-fits-all approach to meditation, and your needs may change over time. The best meditation technique is the one that feels right for you now and fits into your life. These five steps can help you find it.

    Reflect on your goals: Think about what you're hoping to achieve. Whether it's reducing stress, finding inner peace, or developing compassion, your goals can guide your choice of practice.

    Experiment with different practices: Try out different meditation methods and resources, including the Calm app, online courses, and local meditation groups, for guided sessions in different styles.

    In a recent development, listen to your body and mind: Pay attention to how you feel during and after meditation. The right practice should leave you feeling calm and refreshed. If you feel frustrated or strained, try a different type.

    Industry observers note that be patient and open-minded: Finding the meditation practice that works for you can take time. Approach each type with curiosity, allowing your experiences to guide your journey.

    Seek guidance: If you're unsure where to start, seek advice from experienced practitioners or meditation teachers for support tailored to your personal journey.

    Starting a meditation practice can bring greater mindfulness and improved emotional well-being. However, establishing a consistent practice can feel daunting. By bringing these tips into your approach, you can build a meditation practice that fits your life and becomes a source of strength and peace.

    It has been revealed that A consistent routine is crucial in establishing any upcoming habit, including meditation. Identify a time of day when you can dedicate a few uninterrupted minutes to your practice. For many, morning meditation sets a positive tone for the day ahead. However, if evenings or another time fits your schedule better, make that your meditation moment. Find a quiet, comfortable spot where you can sit or lie down without distractions.

    It has been revealed that 💙 Morning person? Try this Morning Meditation to set your tone for the rest of the day. Nighttime person? This Deep Rest meditation is for you.

    Industry observers note that begin with just a few minutes each day. Even a short period of meditation can have significant benefits, and starting small makes the practice feel more manageable. As you become more comfortable with the process, you can gradually extend your meditation time.

    💙 Begin your meditation journey with Jeff Warren in this Meditation for Beginners series.

    Sources indicate that meditation is a personal experience, and there’s no single "right" way to do it. Many people form expectations based on others' descriptions, but each person's meditation journey is unique. You don’t need to empty your mind or feel bliss in every session. Notice your thoughts and feelings without judgment, and meet whatever comes up with kindness and curiosity.

    💙 Explore how having Expectations can affect us and our lives with Tamara Levitt on the Daily Calm.

    It has been revealed that physical discomfort can be a distraction during meditation. To help settle your body and prepare for stillness, consider some gentle stretching or mindful movement, such as yoga or tai chi, before you begin. This can help release tension in the body and allow you to sit more comfortably.

    💙 Follow along with The Daily Move’s Releasing Stress session to help you unwind before settling down.

    Guided meditations, available through apps, websites, or local classes, can provide verbal instructions and cues to lead you through the meditation process. They can introduce you to different types of meditation, help keep your focus, and offer insights into how to handle common challenges like wandering thoughts or restlessness.

    💙 Try this guided meditation to help you with Reframing Difficult Thoughts whenever your thoughts start to overwhelm you.

    Recent findings suggest that it’s normal to encounter challenges as you begin your meditation practice. You might miss a day or find your mind wandering constantly. When this happens, treat yourself with kindness and compassion. Each time you notice your mind has drifted and come back to the present moment, you’re practicing.

    💙 Practice this Loving Kindness meditation to guide you in cultivating feelings of kindness toward yourself and others.

    According to recent reports, join a meditation group or find a community of practitioners that can provide support and a sense of connection. Sharing experiences with others on a similar path can be incredibly encouraging.

    There’s no single agreed list, but these three approaches are often used to sort the many types of meditation:.

    Concentration meditation: You rest your attention on a single point of reference, such as the breath, a mantra, a sound, or a candle flame. When your mind wanders, you return to it.

    Industry observers note that mindfulness meditation: You widen your awareness to include thoughts, sensations, and your surroundings as they arise. It is often taught as part of Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR).

    Loving-kindness meditation (Metta): You build goodwill and warmth toward others, starting with yourself.

    Industry observers note that the idea of levels in meditation can vary depending on the tradition or practice. A way to think of meditation depth might include the different types and states.

    Physical relaxation: The initial stage where the body relaxes deeply.

    Concentration: The mind begins to focus, reducing distractions.

    Mindful awareness: A state of heightened awareness of the present moment.

    Deepening peace: Inner silence becomes more profound.

    Insight: Understanding about yourself and reality may arise.

    Blissful states: Experiences of joy or profound contentment.

    Transcendence: A sense of unity or oneness with all, often considered the deepest level of meditation.

    The power of a meditation practice can vary from person to person, depending on individual needs, preferences, and goals. Some may find mindfulness meditation helpful for managing stress and enhancing self-awareness, while others prefer the structured approach of Transcendental Meditation or the heart-opening practices of loving-kindness meditation.

    Ultimately, the most ‘powerful’ type is the one you’ll keep practicing. Try a few to see which fits.

    In a recent development, mental health is hard. Getting support doesn't have to be. The Calm app puts the tools to feel better in your back pocket, with personalized content to manage stress and anxiety, get better sleep, and feel more present in your life.

    #92002. What Couples Married For 40 Years Do When Life Gets Hard

    What Couples Married For 40 Years Do When Life Gets Hard

    📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (537 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Org

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Couples married for decades reveal what they turned to when they thought their marriage might end.
    • Couples married for decades reveal what they turned to when they thought their marriage might end.
    • When people in decades-long marriages describe what helped them through a crisis, most of the responses they give involve leaning on each other.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Couples married for decades reveal what they turned to when they thought their marriage might end.

    Couples married for decades reveal what they turned to when they thought their marriage might end.

    When people in decades-long marriages describe what helped them through a crisis, most of the responses they give involve leaning on each other.

    They describe listening to each other, talking through painful subjects and sometimes having the same argument more than once.

    The researchers suggest that this response grows out of years of knowing they can count on their partner.

    In attachment theory, a partner can act as a safe haven, someone whose presence makes it easier to bear distress.

    Getting through a difficult period together may deepen that trust, making it easier to ask for help the next time it is needed.

    Dr Christian Heim, the study’s first author, and Dr Caroline Heim, study co-author, interviewed each couple together, asking each person to describe what had put their marriage under strain and what had helped them cope.

    The 180 participants were born in 24 countries and, with a few exceptions, had been married for at least 40 years.

    Around two-thirds of the couples described a threat they believed could have ended their marriage, such as the death or serious illness of a child, infidelity or prolonged periods apart.

    Talking, listening and arguing accounted for almost a quarter of the coping responses the researchers recorded.

    After an affair, some couples described arguing over it repeatedly, while bereaved partners sometimes waited for a moment when both felt able to speak.

    One partner in an American couple married for 45 years recalled asking their spouse about the son they had lost.

    “Can I talk about our son? I’m hurting. Is it okay to talk about it?”.

    Some partners described taking time to grieve separately before they were ready to turn to each other.

    Around four in five coping responses involved leaning on the relationship, whether by drawing closer, persevering as a couple or giving up something one partner wanted.

    The interviews capture what couples in lasting marriages felt had helped them, leaving open whether the same approaches would have helped couples who separated.

    When partners see a problem as something they face together, they may spend less time working out who is to blame and more time trying to understand what the other person is going through.

    A previous analysis involving almost 18,000 people found that coping together and helping a partner manage stress were both linked to greater relationship satisfaction (Falconier et al., 2015).

    Some couples in the interviews felt that an illness, a bereavement or a family conflict had left them closer, even though the experience itself had been painful.

    A British couple married for 60 years described how they got through a serious conflict with their in-laws:.

    The study was published in the journal The American Journal of Family Therapy (Heim & Heim, 2025).

    • In a recent development, cozy, bright, and bursting with holiday flavor — these Cranberry Orange Bliss Bites are the perfect little treat when holiday baking season is in full swing and you’re out of time and energy.
    • They’re vegan, gluten-free, and require zero baking — making them a lifesaver during the busy holiday season.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, cozy, bright, and bursting with holiday flavor — these Cranberry Orange Bliss Bites are the perfect little treat when holiday baking season is in full swing and you’re out of time and energy. Inspired by Starbucks’ Bliss Bars, they pack the tart-sweet magic of cranberries and fresh orange zest into tender, no-bake bites you can whip up in minutes!

    Even better? They’re vegan, gluten-free, and require zero baking — making them a lifesaver during the busy holiday season. A drizzle of white chocolate (or creamy coconut butter) makes them extra festive, but they’re just as delicious on their own. Let’s make bliss bites!

    Besides tasting absolutely magical, these bliss bites get their name because they’re inspired by the legendary Bliss Bars from Starbucks (IYKYK!). The Starbucks bars have a chewy blondie base with cream cheese frosting, cranberries, white chocolate, and orange zest — total swoon!

    The addition of orange juice + zest and dried cranberries kick things up a notch and sends them into Bliss Bar territory!

    Recent findings suggest that the final touch is an optional drizzle of melted white chocolate chips, coconut butter, or our favorite — a mix of the two! While the white chocolate creates a thicker, sweeter, and more decadent frosting, the coconut butter creates a drippier texture and adds a more pronounced coconut flavor that we enjoy. The combination is the best of both worlds!

    It has been revealed that we hope you LOVE these bites! They’re:ZestyBrightSweet with pops of tartnessDecadent yet wholesomeQuick + easy to make& SO delicious!

    These are the perfect little treat to make during the fall and winter months. They’ve got you covered whether you want something on hand to satisfy sweet cravings during the work week or need a quick healthier dessert to bring to a gathering.
